common_name: Jules Dwarf Princess Flower (Dwarf Glory Bush)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in fertile, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact selection needs far less room than seed-grown princess flower and suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and large containers.

directions: 'Jules' is a dwarf, heavily branched selection of princess flower that tops out at roughly a yard tall and wide, a fraction of the size of seed-grown plants, while still producing the same broad clusters of royal-purple, five-petaled flowers above velvety, red-edged foliage. Its naturally tight, rounded habit means little pruning is needed to keep it in bounds, making it a popular choice for mixed borders, patio containers, and low informal hedges along the Gulf Coast. Give it full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates light afternoon shade in the hottest inland gardens, and keep soil consistently moist but well drained. Where winter temperatures dip into the mid-20s Fahrenheit, plants are usually killed to the ground but resprout reliably from the root once the soil warms in spring.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after frost danger has passed, in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil; allow generous room to spread, since established clumps send up root suckers and can colonize a bed over time.

directions: Japanese glorybower carries large, heart-shaped leaves and dense, upright terminal panicles of small, brilliant scarlet-red flowers that open over a long summer-into-fall season, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies to Gulf Coast gardens. It blooms most heavily with a half day of direct sun but appreciates afternoon shade in the hottest, most humid locations, paired with consistently moist, fertile soil. Because it spreads by underground suckers and reseeds readily in mild climates, it has escaped cultivation in parts of peninsular Florida; gardeners outside its hardiness range or near natural areas should site it where suckering can be contained or dig out any wandering shoots each season. Top growth is killed by freezing temperatures, but established clumps typically resprout from the roots once the soil warms the following spring.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium / NC Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot; its multiple arching stems and wide crown need plenty of lateral room, so site it as a specimen or background shrub rather than in a tight bed.

directions: Fountain clerodendrum produces masses of long, slender-tubed white flowers with protruding stamens, held in terminal clusters so dense that a blooming plant resembles a spray of water, which later give way to showy blue-black berries cupped by red bracts. This fast-growing, multi-stemmed shrub forms a wide, V-branched crown and is best used as a background planting, informal screen, or specimen where its mature spread can be accommodated. It performs best in full sun to light shade with regular moisture and rich, well-drained soil, and it tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers without difficulty. Because it is reliably hardy only in the warmest coastal zones, gardeners farther inland typically grow it as a container specimen that is moved under cover before the first hard freeze.
sources: National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web
